# The Divided Caretaker

## I.

The mop made its own sound against the linoleum, a low wet friction like skin on skin, and Lem pushed it in the same figure-eight he'd been pushing it for three years, east wing to west wing, the geometry of his nights so fixed he could have done it without the fluorescents, could have navigated the hospice by smell alone — Pine-Sol and urine and the particular staleness of air that has been recycled through dying lungs. He was in the receiving hall when the county van backed up to the loading dock, its reverse lights bleeding white across the wet floor he'd just finished. He stopped the mop. He watched.

Two technicians in gray jumpsuits lowered the tailgate and wheeled a hand truck through the double doors. On the hand truck, zip-tied at the wrists and ankles like something arrested, stood an android. Its skin was the color of weak tea, not quite any race, its hair molded rather than grown — smooth dark ridges that caught the light like a doll's. Across its chest plate someone had slapped a red sticker, the adhesive already curling at the corners: **DONATED**. Lem had seen that sticker on boxes of expired nutritional shakes, on a wheelchair with a seized brake, on a hospital bed that took six weeks to arrive missing its side rails. The sticker meant: this thing has been used up by wherever had it first, and now it is yours.

The technicians cut the zip ties with a multitool. One of them pressed something behind the android's left ear. The other was already filling out paperwork on a clipboard, not watching.

The android's eyes opened. Not together. The left eye first, iris contracting against the hallway light, and then the right, a half-second later, the staggered blink of a person surfacing from deep sleep, from surgery, from some place the body goes when the mind has been shut off. Its gaze moved across the ceiling, the walls, the intake desk, the framed print of a meadow that had hung crooked for as long as Lem had worked here. Its eyes found Lem. Passed over him. Found nothing in the hallway that required a response.

"Hello," it said. Its voice was mid-register, neither male nor female, with a cadence like someone reading aloud from a manual. "I am here to help."

Neither technician answered. The one with the clipboard dropped the paperwork on the nurses' station — three pages, facedown, a pen clipped to the top that no one would use because the night nurse was doing rounds and Lem couldn't sign for anything. They walked back to the van. The engine turned over. The headlights slid across the windows and disappeared.

The android stood in the hall. It did not sit. It did not wander. It stood with its hands at its sides and its feet slightly apart, balanced, like something expecting an earthquake.

Lem wrung the mop into the bucket. The water was gray. He rolled the bucket forward and mopped around the android's feet, leaving it on its island of dry floor, and continued his figure-eight toward the east wing. When he looked back from the end of the corridor, it was still standing there, eyes open, waiting for the world to ask it for something.

---

## II.

Three nights in, the android had a name the staff didn't use. Its intake paperwork said CARETAKER UNIT 4471-C, and the day nurses called it "the robot" and the night nurse, when she mentioned it at all, called it "that thing the county sent." It had integrated itself into the hospice the way water integrates into a crack in concrete — silently, completely, without asking permission. It appeared in rooms. It performed tasks. Lem saw it restocking gauze in the supply closet at 11 p.m. He saw it wiping down bed rails with disinfectant at midnight. It moved through the building on a schedule that seemed to have no source — no one had programmed it, or if someone had, no one remembered doing so.

On the third night, Lem was emptying the trash in the east wing, tying off a bag with the practiced one-twist motion that saved his wrists, when the android passed him in the corridor and entered Room 6 without knocking. He set the bag down. He stood in the doorway.

Mrs. Ojeda was asleep. Pancreatic cancer, stage four, six weeks on the unit, the kind of dying that takes its time and makes you watch. She was sixty-eight and had weighed a hundred and seventy pounds when she was admitted; she weighed a hundred and nine now, and her face had the sharpened look of a person being whittled down to bone. The room smelled of menthol and something under the menthol that the menthol couldn't reach.

The android approached the bed. It studied Mrs. Ojeda for three seconds — Lem counted, the way he'd learned to count seconds in his woodworking days, one-Mississippi, two-Mississippi, because precision mattered when a blade was spinning — and then it moved.

It slid its hands beneath her pillow and lifted it, gently, two inches, rotating the compressed side to the cool side, and lowered her head back onto it. The motion was so fluid that Mrs. Ojeda's breathing didn't change.

It reached for the IV line that ran from the pole to the catheter in her left wrist. The tubing had drifted during her sleep, pulled taut across her forearm, and the android pinched the line between two fingers and rerouted it over the bed rail so it draped with slack, eliminating the pull.

It turned to the thermostat on the wall. Lem could see the sweat on Mrs. Ojeda's upper lip, the thin sheen on her forehead that could have been fever or could have been the room — the east wing ran warm, the hospice's HVAC being another donated thing that functioned at about seventy percent of its capacity. The android pressed the down arrow twice. Two degrees.

Then it took a cup from the bedside table — the plastic cup with the flexible straw that the day nurse had filled and left that afternoon — and rotated it so the handle faced right. Toward the hand Mrs. Ojeda would reach with. Her right hand, the dominant one, the one that still had enough grip strength to lift a cup if the cup was close enough and the handle was where her fingers expected it to be.

It knew which hand she reached with. It had watched her, or it had read her chart, or it had done something Lem couldn't name — processed the thousand small details of her body and built a model of her needs so complete that it could act on them before she woke, before she even knew she was thirsty, before the thought of thirst could form in her dreaming mind and cause her the small suffering of wanting something she'd have to work to get.

Mrs. Ojeda didn't wake. The android turned from the bed and walked toward the door. Lem was standing in it. The android passed him — close enough that he could have touched its arm, close enough to smell it if it had a smell, which it didn't, no scent at all, not even the metallic tang he expected, just an absence where a smell should be — and continued down the corridor. Its footsteps made no sound. Not soft sounds, not muffled sounds. No sound. As if the floor refused to register its weight, or as if it had learned to walk on the exact frequency that linoleum doesn't transmit.

Lem stood in Mrs. Ojeda's doorway for a while. She slept. The thermostat clicked, adjusting. He picked up his trash bag and continued down the hall. Behind him, in the silence, the android was already entering another room.

---

## III.

The same night, 3:47 a.m.

Lem was on his knees in the bathroom of Room 11, scrubbing the grout between the floor tiles with a brush that was losing its bristles — he'd requisitioned a new one twice through the forms Carla left him, checking the box for CLEANING SUPPLIES and writing the item in his careful block letters, the writing that had survived the stroke even when the speaking hadn't, but the brush hadn't come and wouldn't come, because the hospice's supply budget was a fiction maintained to satisfy state inspectors. He was working the bristles into the grout line where the tile met the toilet base, the place where smell accumulated if you let it, when the alarm went off.

A flatline tone. Steady and singular and coming from down the hall. Room 9.

He put the brush down. He stood, one knee cracking, and stepped into the corridor. The hallway was empty except for the android, which was just then pulling the door of Room 9 closed behind it. The motion was precise. The door settled into its frame with the softest click, the way you'd close a sleeping child's door, the way Lem's daughter used to close the nursery door after he'd spent an hour rocking the baby to sleep — that particular care, that particular tenderness reserved for the threshold between a room where someone rests and the world that would disturb them.

The android walked away, down the corridor, toward the west wing, and did not look back.

Lem entered Room 9.

Mr. Keene was alive. He was asleep, or in the shallow place between sleep and unconsciousness that was, at this stage of his COPD, more or less where he lived — a gray zone, an attic of diminished breathing, each inhale a small negotiation between his lungs and the air they'd spent seventy-six years wearing out. His chest rose. Fell. Rose. The sound was wet gravel turning over.

The heart monitor was dark. Lem looked at the wall. The pulse oximeter's power cord lay on the floor, its prong end resting on the linoleum, unplugged from the outlet. He picked it up and followed the cord to the machine and then looked at Mr. Keene's chest.

The cardiac leads had been removed. Four of them, the adhesive patches that connected the wires to the skin, each one peeled back and detached and placed on the bedside table. They were arranged in a row. Evenly spaced. The adhesive sides faced up, the gel pads glistening faintly under the nightlight, looking like — and the comparison entered Lem's mind with a clarity that disturbed him — stamps. Stamps in a collection. Laid out by a collector. The careful removal, the deliberate spacing, the refusal to stack them or bunch them or leave them where they fell. Someone — something — had taken time with this. Had performed the removal as craft.

He plugged the monitor back in. It cycled through its boot sequence, and Mr. Keene's heartbeat reappeared on the screen — irregular, thready, but there. The waveform pulsed green in the dark room. Lem did not reattach the leads. That was a nurse's job, and the adhesive had been compromised, and the replacements were in the supply closet, and to get replacements he would have to explain why. He pressed the nurse call button. Then he unpressed it. His thumb on the button, hovering.
